title: Why chatbots miscount letters in a word
summary: Models read tokens, not spelled-out letters. A 2024 study found they can tell which letters are present but fail at counting repeats.

beats.say: Language models write essays, yet struggle to count letters in a word.
Most models do not read text as letters. They read tokens.
A tokenizer cuts text into pieces before the model sees it.
Here is one real tokenizer, Bert base uncased, from the Hugging Face docs.
It splits the word G.P.U. into two pieces.
Another tokenizer splits Transformers into Transform and ers.
Pieces hide spelling, but a twenty twenty four study found a stronger pattern.
Models could tell which letters were present. They failed at counting them.
beats.cap: Recognize letters: yes. Count them: no.

rows.text: Which letters are in the word

beats.say: Most models failed once a letter appeared more than twice.
beats.cap: More than two repeats: most models fail

beats.say: Tokens hide letters, and counting is the harder part.

facts.claim: Hugging Face's tokenizer documentation shows bert-base-uncased splitting the word 'GPU' into the pieces 'gp' and '##u'
facts.note: HF Transformers docs, Summary of the tokenizers: BertTokenizer google-bert/bert-base-uncased tokenizes 'I have a new GPU!' into i, have, a, new, gp, ##u, !

facts.claim: The same documentation shows xlnet-base-cased splitting 'Transformers' into 'Transform' and 'ers'
facts.note: HF docs: XLNetTokenizer xlnet/xlnet-base-cased splits the rare word 'Transformers' into 'Transform' and 'ers'

facts.claim: A December 2024 arXiv study found models can recognize the letters in a word but not count them
facts.note: arXiv 2412.18626 abstract: 'models are capable of recognizing the letters but not counting them'; first version posted 19 December 2024

facts.claim: The study found most models fail on words where a letter appears more than twice, and attributes the problem to the complexity of counting
facts.note: arXiv 2412.18626 abstract: strongest correlation with letters appearing more than once; most models fail when letters appear more than twice; authors conclude the problem stems from counting complexity
